transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?
Since my husband’s heart attack, it’s like I’m not really here. When I walk into his hospital room, everything feels unreal, like I’m watching it happen to someone else.

Did this unreal, detached feeling start right after your husband’s heart attack and stay only around that event, or have you had similar episodes at other times too? About how long does each episode last?

No, I’ve never felt anything like this before; it only started after my husband collapsed six days ago. It happens whenever I walk into his ICU room or even when I'm just sitting in my own living room. I'm not really sure how long each episode lasts, but it just comes on during those times and everything feels far away.

Since your husband’s heart attack, have you also had other stress reactions like intense anxiety, being constantly on edge, trouble sleeping, or repeated upsetting memories of what happened? Or is the main problem just the unreal, detached feeling?

The detached feeling is a big part of it, but it's definitely not the only thing. I keep seeing his face turn blue and hearing that awful gurgling sound popping into my head out of nowhere, like I'm right back at that kitchen table. I'm also constantly on edge, and every little noise, like a hospital monitor beeping, makes me jump out of my skin.

Since these symptoms started six days ago, have they been getting better, staying about the same, or getting worse? And have they caused major problems in your daily functioning, like not being able to work, sleep, or take care of yourself?

They’ve stayed about the same, just a constant, heavy blankness that hasn't let up at all over these past six days. It’s completely disrupted my life—I’ve stopped going to my quilting circle, skipped my own doctor appointments, and I can't even manage simple things like paying bills or cooking because I can't organize my thoughts or leave his bedside.

final_diagnosis.reason: Symptoms began immediately after a severe traumatic stressor (witnessing her husband's heart attack) and have persisted for 6 days, within the time frame for acute stress reaction. She reports dissociative unreality/detachment, intrusive re-experiencing, hyperarousal/startle, and marked functional disruption. The presentation is too early for PTSD and is directly linked to the recent trauma rather than a primary dissociative disorder.
